analysis.one_liner: Bans hidden spread pricing and reimbursement clawbacks by pharmacy benefit managers and forces disclosure of their drug-pricing fees.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to require pharmacy benefit managers to disclose how they charge for prescription drugs was introduced with 15 Senate backers and has sat in the Senate Commerce Committee since February 2025 without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are middlemen that negotiate drug prices and pay pharmacies on behalf of health plans. This bill would make it illegal for a PBM to charge a health plan more for a drug than it pays the pharmacy and keep the difference, and to arbitrarily claw back money it owes pharmacies. PBMs could avoid those bans only if they pass 100% of rebates and discounts back to health plans and fully disclose every fee, markup, and manufacturer rebate they receive. The bill also requires annual public reporting to the Federal Trade Commission, directs studies of PBM market power and formulary practices, protects whistleblowers, and lets both the FTC and state attorneys general enforce the rules with civil penalties up to $1 million.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who fill prescriptions, employers and unions that buy health coverage, independent and community pharmacies that currently bear surprise reimbursement cuts, and taxpayers who help fund Medicare and Medicaid drug costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, pharmacies, and employers buying coverage

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for a PBM to charge a health plan more for a drug's cost or dispensing fee than it reimburses the pharmacy and keep the difference (spread pricing), unless the PBM passes 100% of price concessions back to the plan and fully discloses its fees and rebates.
It bans PBM practices of arbitrarily reducing, rescinding, or clawing back reimbursement owed to pharmacies, and of lowering pharmacy reimbursement to offset federal reimbursement changes.

PBMs must report annually to the FTC and HHS on the difference between what plans paid them and what they paid pharmacies, fees charged to pharmacies, clawbacks, reasons for moving drugs to costlier formulary tiers, and any favorable treatment of pharmacies they own.

The FTC must report annually to Congress on its enforcement actions and complaints, analyze whether PBM practices lead to mergers or monopoly, and report on whether formulary placement raises PBM revenue without lowering patient cost; the Government Accountability Office must study PBM market share, rebate flows, and effects on consumer drug costs.

Employees and contractors of PBMs, insurers, pharmacies, and drug manufacturers who report violations are protected from retaliation, can sue for reinstatement and double back pay, and cannot be forced into predispute arbitration for these claims.

The FTC enforces the ban on unfair or deceptive practices with civil penalties up to $1 million (each day of a continuing violation counts separately), and state attorneys general may sue on behalf of their residents.

analysis.who_pays: The large PBMs — many owned by insurance companies — would give up spread-pricing margins, undisclosed fees, and clawbacks, and would bear the cost of annual disclosure and potential FTC and state penalties. Some of those compliance costs could show up in plan administrative fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: The three dominant PBMs and their parent insurers

drawbacks.text: Transparency and compliance rules carry real costs: PBMs would have to build systems for annual fee and rebate reporting to federal agencies, and opponents argue these administrative costs could be passed through to health plans and premiums.

The bill regulates conduct and disclosure rather than capping drug prices directly, so it relies on the FTC and lawsuits to change behavior, and PBMs can keep their current pricing models if they pass through all rebates and disclose all fees — meaning the market could remain concentrated with three dominant middlemen.

The bill includes an affirmative defense allowing PBMs to justify reimbursement reductions as necessary to comply with law or protect patient safety or access, giving regulated companies a basis to contest enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who buy prescriptions or coverage, the upside is concrete: the bill targets the least-visible points in the drug pricing chain — the spread between what plans pay and what pharmacies receive, and clawbacks from pharmacies — and mandates disclosure of manufacturer rebates that today stay hidden. The costs are administrative and fall mainly on the regulated companies. The honest limitation is that transparency does not by itself guarantee lower prices; enforcement by the FTC and state attorneys general will determine whether the disclosure changes behavior.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has had no hearing, markup, or floor action so far this Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Grassley introduced the Pharmacy Benefit Manager Transparency Act of 2025 on February 11, 2025, joined by 11 original cosponsors including Sen. Maria Cantwell, the Commerce Committee's ranking Democrat.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on February 11, 2025, and no further action appears in the record.
The bill has gathered 14 cosponsors beyond its sponsor, split 8 Republicans and 6 Democrats, giving it bipartisan support but no committee or floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the dominant PBMs and their parent insurers: no rule change has taken effect, and the bill's lack of committee movement means their current pricing practices continue unchanged.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is bipartisan: the sponsor is Republican and the bill's 15 total supporters include 8 Republicans, 6 Democrats, and 1 Independent; no recorded opposition appears in the congressional record.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (the three dominant firms and their insurer parents)
industries.note: PBMs currently profit from the spread between what health plans pay and what pharmacies receive, from fees charged to pharmacies, and from undisclosed manufacturer rebates; the bill bans keeping the spread, bans clawbacks unless conditions are met, and requires full fee and rebate disclosure with FTC penalties up to $1 million per violation.

The bill bans arbitrary reimbursement clawbacks and forced reimbursement cuts, and requires PBMs to report favorable treatment of pharmacies they own — addressing practices that push independent pharmacies toward insolvency.

As health plans and payers, insurers gain from requirements that PBMs pass through rebates and disclose fees, but the three largest insurers own major PBMs, so the disclosure rules cut into their vertical profits.

Manufacturers would have the rebates and fees they pay PBMs publicly aggregated in annual reporting and GAO studies, but the bill does not directly regulate manufacturer list prices; the GAO study of whether formularies favor high-rebate drugs could pressure their rebate strategy.

industries.industry: Employers and other health plan sponsors
industries.note: As payers, employers gain visibility into what their PBMs actually charge versus pay, information the bill requires be disclosed in every PBM contract.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Commerce Committee, whose ranking member is a cosponsor — a favorable position for a hearing or markup. An earlier version of this same Grassley-Cantwell legislation advanced through the committee in the previous Congress but never received a full Senate vote, and PBM regulation faces competing, broader drug-pricing bills; without committee action and floor time, it is likely to stall again this Congress.
